title: TSMC Weighs 3D DRAM Push at Nvidia's Request
author: F
text:
F

Fred Chen
Moderator

Foundry Giant Studies Memory Entry as Nvidia Seeks to Diversify SupplyAfter Foundry and Advanced Packaging, Memory Could Bring New Rival to Korean Chipmakers

Published 2026.11.07. 11:29:44

By Kim Hye-rankhr@sedaily.com

TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, is studying plans to produce 3D DRAM, a next-generation memory technology, at the request of Nvidia. The move would expand the Taiwanese company into a business it has long stayed out of. If TSMC proceeds to mass production, Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS) would face a new rival in a memory market they have dominated.

TSMC recently began reviewing plans to manufacture 3D DRAM after a request from Nvidia, its largest customer, U.S. technology outlet The Information reported on the 7th, citing two people familiar with the matter. The company is examining options including building a new memory plant or acquiring an existing facility and converting it for production, according to the report. No decisions have been made on whether to invest, how much to spend or when output would begin.

Memory Entry Studied Amid AI Supply Crunch as Nvidia Diversifies Sourcing

The move comes as surging demand for AI chips has deepened a shortage of memory. Competition to secure high-performance memory to support computing workloads has intensified along with demand for graphics processing units. Nvidia's request to TSMC is seen as an attempt to diversify its sources and build a more stable base for component supply.

The 3D DRAM technology under review stacks memory cells vertically to raise storage density. It differs structurally from high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, which stacks multiple DRAM chips to increase data transfer speeds.

Producing memory in-house would further strengthen TSMC's influence over the AI chip supply chain. Nvidia's GPUs are currently manufactured by TSMC, while the HBM mounted on them is supplied by SK hynix, Samsung Electronics and others. If TSMC succeeds in memory production, a single company could cover everything from GPU manufacturing to memory and advanced packaging. That would let it control the entire supply chain from GPU manufacturing to memory and packaging, rather than depend on outside memory suppliers.

A Medium- to Long-Term Variable for Korea's Two Memory Leaders

The development could become a competitive factor for Korean memory makers over the medium to long term. The chip industry has long been split along clear lines, with Taiwan leading foundry services and Korea leading memory. TSMC has built overwhelming competitiveness in foundry but has not entered memory production directly. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, by contrast, have accumulated technology and mass-production experience in DRAM and HBM.

If TSMC adds memory, existing customers could source memory and foundry services from a single supplier, which could affect the bargaining power of the Korean companies. The possibility that TSMC extends the customer base it has built in foundry and advanced packaging into memory is another risk factor.

Still, the Korean companies' positions are unlikely to be shaken soon. Stacking memory cells vertically leaves unresolved technical hurdles such as heat generation and process integration, and it could take years to achieve stable yields and a mass-production system. Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and U.S.-based Micron are also developing the technology, making it difficult for TSMC to close the technology gap quickly.

"If TSMC's entry into memory becomes a reality, it could become a new competitive factor for Korean companies," an industry official said. "Securing an early lead in next-generation memory technology and stable mass-production capability will become more important."
